claim: The dorsoventral boundary of leaves defines an axis of symmetry through the centre of the organ separating the top (dorsal) and bottom (ventral) tissues.
source: In plants the dorsoventral boundary of leaves defines an axis of symmetry through the centre of the organ separating the top (dorsal) and bottom (ventral) tissues.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about plant leaf anatomy.

claim: The positioning of the dorsoventral boundary is critical for leaf morphogenesis.
source: Although the positioning of this boundary is critical for leaf morphogenesis, how the boundary is established and how it influences development remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Leaf orientation, morphology and position are pre-patterned by HD-ZIPIII and KAN gene expression in the shoot.
source: Using live-imaging and perturbation experiments we show that leaf orientation, morphology and position are pre-patterned by HD-ZIPIII and KAN gene expression in the shoot
evidence: This claim is supported by live-imaging and perturbation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Dorsoventral genes coordinate to regulate plant development by localizing auxin response between their expression domains.
source: leading to a model in which dorsoventral genes coordinate to regulate plant development by localizing auxin response between their expression domains.
evidence: This is presented as a model derived from the experimental data.

claim: Auxin levels feedback on dorsoventral patterning by spatially organizing HD-ZIPIII and KAN expression in the shoot periphery.
source: However we also find that auxin levels feedback on dorsoventral patterning by spatially organizing HD-ZIPIII and KAN expression in the shoot periphery.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: The regulation of HD-ZIPIII and KAN genes by auxin governs their response to wounds.
source: By demonstrating that the regulation of these genes by auxin also governs their response to wounds, our results also provide a parsimonious explanation for the influence of wounds on leaf dorsoventrality.
evidence: This is stated as a demonstrated finding from the experiments.

claim: Lateral organ development in plants involves organ positioning, specification of different cell types, and organ morphogenesis occurring in a coordinated manner.
source: Lateral organ development in plants and animals typically involves several processes occurring in a coordinated manner. These include organ positioning, the specification of different cell types and organ morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about plant development.

claim: Plant organs such as leaves arise continuously in regular patterns around the shoot apical meristem (SAM).
source: Unlike animals however, plant organs such as leaves arise continuously in regular patterns around the shoot apical meristem (SAM).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about plant development.

claim: Leaves are restricted to the meristem periphery.
source: Nevertheless, certain features of leaves are relatively constant including the restriction of their formation to the meristem periphery
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about leaf development.

claim: Leaves have a flattened, dorsoventral (top-bottom) orientation with respect to the shoot apex.
source: Nevertheless, certain features of leaves are relatively constant including the restriction of their formation to the meristem periphery and their flattened, dorsoventral (top-bottom) orientation with respect to the shoot apex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about leaf development.

claim: Wounding experiments involving the isolation of leaf primordia from the meristem have suggested the presence of an inductive signal from the meristem that promotes dorsal identity within leaf primordia at the time of organ initiation.
source: Since the 1950s wounding experiments involving the isolation of leaf primordia from the meristem have suggested the presence of an inductive signal from the meristem that promotes dorsal identity within leaf primordia at the time of organ initiation (Reinhardt et al., 2005; Sussex, 1951).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transient auxin depletion in the adaxial tissues of leaf primordia promotes dorsal identity.
source: A variant on this theme is the proposal that transient auxin depletion in the adaxial (adjacent to the shoot axis) tissues of leaf primordia promotes dorsal identity (Qi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Dorsoventral patterning is pre-established, being directly derived from central-peripheral patterning of the shoot.
source: In contrast, other studies suggest that dorsoventral patterning is pre-established, being directly derived from central-peripheral patterning of the shoot (Hagemann and Gleissberg, 1996; Husbands et al., 2009; Kerstetter et al., 2001; Koch and Meinhardt, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcription factors involved in both dorsal and ventral cell fate in the leaf are expressed in the SAM in a central and peripheral manner respectively.
source: Supporting this proposal is the observation that transcription factors involved in both dorsal and ventral cell fate in the leaf are expressed in the SAM in a central and peripheral manner respectively (Emery et al., 2003; Kerstetter et al., 2001; McConnell et al., 2001; Yadav et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The manner in which leaf dorsoventrality is first established in leaves remains unresolved.
source: Thus, the manner in which leaf dorsoventrality is first established in leaves remains unresolved (Kuhlemeier and Timmermans, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Tissues located along the boundary between dorsal and ventral leaf tissues act as organizers by producing mobile signals that pattern lamina growth.
source: To explain how leaf dorsoventrality regulates morphogenesis, Waites and Hudson, 1995 took a cue from wing development in Drosophila (Diaz-Benjumea and Cohen, 1993) and proposed that tissues located along the boundary between dorsal and ventral leaf tissues, i.e. along the leaf margin, act as organizers by producing mobile signals that pattern lamina growth (Waites and Hudson, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KLUH is expressed along the dorsoventral boundary.
source: So far, several genes have been identified that are expressed along this boundary including KLUH (Anastasiou et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: WOX1, WOX2 and PRS are expressed along the dorsoventral boundary.
source: So far, several genes have been identified that are expressed along this boundary including KLUH (Anastasiou et al., 2007) and the WOX family transcription WOX1, WOX2 and PRS (Haecker et al., 2004; Matsumoto and Okada, 2001; Nakata et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: WOX genes are required for proper lamina growth.
source: The WOX genes in particular are required for proper lamina growth but are expressed only at the boundary region suggesting they may promote long-range patterning (Nakata et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ectopic expression of WOX genes can cause filamentous outgrowths at the leaf base, but overall lamina growth is fairly normal.
source: However although their ectopic expression can cause filamentous outgrowths at the leaf base, overall lamina growth is fairly normal (Nakata et al., 2012) suggesting that additional factors must direct patterning.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: WOX genes regulate the expression of both dorsal and ventrally expressed transcription factors and miRNAs.
source: The WOX genes are also known to regulate the expression of both dorsal and ventrally expressed transcription factors and miRNAs (Nakata et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: WOX genes promote lamina growth at least in part by maintaining the integrity of dorsal and ventral expression domains.
source: The WOX genes are also known to regulate the expression of both dorsal and ventrally expressed transcription factors and miRNAs (Nakata et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017) indicating that the WOX genes promote lamina growth at least in part by maintaining the integrity of dorsal and ventral expression domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies.

claim: Arabidopsis plants mutant for the KANADI (KAN) genes develop leaves ectopically from the hypocotyl and leaf tissues.
source: For instance, Arabidopsis plants mutant for the KANADI (KAN) genes develop leaves ectopically from the hypocotyl and leaf tissues (Izhaki and Bowman, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Plants mutant for the Class III HD-ZIP (HD-ZIPIII) genes develop leaves from the center of the shoot.
source: while plants mutant for the Class III HD-ZIP (HD-ZIPIII) genes develop leaves from the center of the shoot (Emery et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The dorsal Class III HD-ZIP protein REVOLUTA (REV) is detected centrally in the shoot apical meristem.
source: In general, we found proteins involved in leaf dorsoventrality to be localized in non-overlapping concentric patterns with the dorsal Class III HD-ZIP protein REVOLUTA (REV) (Otsuga et al., 2001) being detected centrally, as marked by the expression of REVp::REV-2 × YPet (REV-2 × YPet)
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ventral protein KANADI1 (KAN1) is expressed peripherally in the shoot apical meristem.
source: and the ventral protein KANADI1 (KAN1) (Kerstetter et al., 2001) expressed peripherally, as marked by the expression of KAN1p::KAN1−2 × GFP (KAN1−2 × GFP) (Figure 1, A to E).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 1.

claim: REV and KAN1 expression domains encircle the meristem and extend contiguously around initiating leaves and floral bracts.
source: These concentric domains not only encircled the meristem but also extended contiguously around initiating leaves and floral bracts.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data described in the text.

claim: Regions of high PIN1-CFP expression, marking positions of organ inception, are centered on a narrow region or 'gap' located between the dorsal and ventral domains.
source: Imaging PIN1p::PIN1-CFP (PIN1-CFP) (Gordon et al., 2007a) together with these reporters revealed regions of high PIN1-CFP expression, marking positions of organ inception (Heisler et al., 2005; Reinhardt et al., 2003), to be centered on a narrow region or 'gap' located between the dorsal and ventral domains (Figure 1D–K).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: REV expression extends out into the PIN1-marked primordia over time.
source: As found previously, REV expression extended out into the PIN1-marked primordia over time (Heisler et al., 2005), reducing the 'gap' between the REV and KAN domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F,M–P).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to a previous study.

claim: At later stages a more substantial 'gap' reappears between the REV and KAN1 domains.
source: Nevertheless, at later stages a more substantial 'gap' reappeared between the REV and KAN1 domains (Figure 1C and D insets; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–L and Q–R) indicating that the distance between the REV and KAN1 domains can change dynamically.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Few cells alter their KAN1 expression during early stages of organ development.
source: Time-lapse imaging revealed that few cells alter their KAN1 expression during these early stages (Figure 2A–F)
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The boundary of KAN1 expression in the SAM marks cells destined to form the future dorsoventral boundary of the organ.
source: suggesting that the boundary of KAN1 expression in the SAM marks cells destined to form the future dorsoventral boundary of the organ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Ventrally expressed MIR165/166 is active in the SAM periphery.
source: Ventrally expressed MIR165/166 (Kidner and Martienssen, 2004; Merelo et al., 2016; Nogueira et al., 2007; Yao et al., 2009) also appeared active in the SAM periphery as marked by a MIR166Ap::GFPER reporter and MIR165/166 biosensor (Figure 3A–I), consistent with previous studies (Miyashima et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 3 and citations to previous studies.

claim: KAN1−2 × GFP and MIR166Ap::GFPER re-establish their expression in the SAM periphery after organ outgrowth.
source: Both KAN1−2 × GFP and MIR166Ap::GFPER re-established their expression in the SAM periphery after organ outgrowth (Figure 1E arrowhead; Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,K and L and Figure 3C arrowhead).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 3.

claim: 2 × GFP-WOX1 expression is limited to the margins and middle domain of leaves and absent in the inflorescence meristem.
source: We found that although 2 × GFP-WOX1 expression was limited to the margins and middle domain of leaves (Figure 4A and B) and absent in the inflorescence meristem (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 4.

claim: In the vegetative shoot PRS-2 ×GFP expression extends from the leaf middle domain to surround the SAM in a region between the KAN1 and REV expression domains.
source: in the vegetative shoot PRS-2 ×GFP expression extended from the leaf middle domain to surround the SAM in a region between the KAN1 and REV expression domains (Figure 4D–H).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 4.

claim: In the inflorescence meristem, PRS-2 × GFP expression is restricted to early cryptic bract primordia.
source: In the inflorescence meristem however, PRS-2 × GFP expression was restricted to early cryptic bract primordia (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 4.

claim: FILp::dsRED-N7 marker is expressed in both the abaxial and adaxial regions of the primordium at inception.
source: In contrast to all genes described so far, a FILp::dsRED-N7 marker was expressed in both the abaxial (away from the shoot axis) and adaxial regions of the primordium at inception, consistent with a previous study (Tameshige et al., 2013) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 5 and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Dorsoventral patterning within young leaf primordia corresponds to and is contiguous with the patterning of dorsoventral gene expression in the SAM.
source: Overall these data reveal that in many respects although not all, dorsoventral patterning within young leaf primordia, including the middle region (Nakata et al., 2012), corresponds to and is contiguous with, the patterning of dorsoventral gene expression in the SAM.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the imaging data presented.

claim: Ectopic expression of MIR165/166-resistant REVr-2 ×VENUS throughout the epidermis causes an arrest of organ formation and repression of KAN1−2 × GFP in both the vegetative and inflorescence meristems.
source: To distinguish between these possibilities we induced the expression of MIR165/166-resistant REVr-2 ×VENUS throughout the epidermis using a pOp6/LhGR two-component (Samalova et al., 2005) system with the ATML1 promoter (Sessions et al., 1999) driving LhGR and found that it caused an arrest of organ formation and repression of KAN1−2 × GFP in both the vegetative and inflorescence meristems (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Despite the lack of organs after REVr-2 ×VENUS induction, stem growth for the inflorescence meristem continues without any obvious change to meristem size.
source: Despite the lack of organs, stem growth for the inflorescence meristem continued without any obvious change to meristem size, indicating that the phenotype initially influenced organ initiation (inset in Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Induction of a short tandem target mimicry construct designed to repress MIR165/166 activity causes similar organ arrest phenotype as REVr-2 ×VENUS induction.
source: Similar results were observed after induction of a short tandem target mimicry construct designed to repress MIR165/166 activity (Yan et al., 2012) (Figure 6F and G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Epidermal induction of MIR165/166-resistant PHAVOLUTA causes organ arrest.
source: or after epidermal induction of MIR165/166-resistant PHAVOLUTA (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Plants expressing KAN1 ectopically in the epidermis stop making new organs.
source: Similarly, plants expressing KAN1 ectopically in the epidermis also stopped making new organs (Figure 6K and L)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The inflorescence meristem takes on a dome shape before eventually arresting after ectopic KAN1 expression.
source: and the inflorescence meristem took on a dome shape before eventually arresting (Figure 6M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Both the KAN and Class III HD-ZIP genes regulate organ positioning at least in part by repressing organ initiation where they are expressed.
source: We conclude both the KAN and Class III HD-ZIP genes regulate organ positioning at least in part by repressing organ initiation where they are expressed.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: After KAN1−2 × GFP induction at the center of the SAM, new organs form ectopically at the perimeter of an enlarged and irregular central domain of induced KAN1−2 × GFP expression.
source: After KAN1−2 × GFP induction, most seedlings initiated several new leaves before their growth stopped. Confocal imaging of seedlings five days after stratification (DAS) on dexamethasone (DEX) induction medium revealed that new organs, marked by high levels of PIN1-CFP expression, formed ectopically at the perimeter of an enlarged and irregular central domain of induced KAN1−2 × GFP expression, in which REV-2 × YPet expression had been repressed (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Ectopic KAN1−2 × GFP is only detected within or bordering organs during their initiation while REV-2 × YPet expression is often restricted during later developmental stages.
source: Although endogenous KAN1 was not monitored, ectopic KAN1−2 × GFP was only detected within or bordering organs during their initiation while REV-2 × YPet expression was often restricted during later developmental stages (Figure 7C–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Patterns of KAN1 gene expression within the SAM can influence subsequent organ development.
source: This indicates that patterns of KAN1 gene expression within the SAM can influence subsequent organ development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The distal margins of developing leaf primordia always correlate with boundaries of REV expression within the epidermis.
source: In particular, we noted that the distal margins of developing leaf primordia always correlated with boundaries of REV expression within the epidermis, even when REV expression was abnormally restricted (arrow heads in Figure 7C–H; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7 and Video 1.

claim: The number and orientation of HD-ZIPIII-KAN boundaries within organ founder cells determines the configuration of later leaf marginal tissue.
source: Specifically, we infer that the number and orientation of boundaries within organ founder cells (as specified by high auxin levels) determines the configuration of later leaf marginal tissue (Figure 7P–S).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and presented as a model in Figure 7.

claim: In the inflorescence meristem the auxin transcriptional marker DR5 is only responsive to auxin in the shoot periphery.
source: In support of this proposal it has been reported that in the inflorescence meristem the auxin transcriptional marker DR5 is only responsive to auxin in the shoot periphery (de Reuille et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In mock-treated seedlings DR5 is expressed at the locations of incipient primordia and at the distal tip of existing leaf primordia.
source: In mock-treated seedlings we found DR5 to be expressed at the locations of incipient primordia and at the distal tip of existing leaf primordia (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8.

claim: NPA-treated seedlings express DR5 in a ring encircling the SAM prior to organ emergence and in the middle domain or dorsoventral boundary region of developing leaves.
source: In contrast, NPA-treated seedlings expressed DR5 in a ring encircling the SAM prior to organ emergence and in the middle domain or dorsoventral boundary region of developing leaves (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8.

claim: The ratiometric R2D2 intracellular auxin reporter reveals a generally broader distribution of auxin compared to the DR5 transcriptional response.
source: Similar experiments with seedlings expressing the ratiometric R2D2 intracellular auxin reporter (Liao et al., 2015) revealed a generally broader distribution of auxin compared to the DR5 transcriptional response, especially after NPA treatment, where signal was not restricted to the meristem periphery or leaf tip (Figure 8E–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Auxin transcriptional response outside the periphery of the vegetative meristem appears repressed.
source: These results indicate that like the inflorescence meristem, auxin transcriptional response outside the periphery of the vegetative meristem appears repressed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: PRS and WOX1 are auxin inducible.
source: Since we also observed PRS expression localized to the meristem periphery (Figure 4D), we tested whether PRS as well as WOX1 are auxin inducible and found that both genes respond to auxin treatment within 12 and 15 hr respectively although their response was restricted to the boundary region (Figure 8I–P).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8.

claim: The auxin response for PRS and WOX1 occurs at the transcriptional level.
source: Measuring transcript levels using qPCR indicated that the auxin response for both genes occurs at the transcriptional level (Figure 8Q).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 8Q.

claim: KAN and HD-ZIPIII genes repress auxin response where they are expressed, leaving a narrow domain of auxin responsive cells in between their expression domains.
source: Considering our results altogether and the finding that KAN1 represses PRS and WOX1 in ventral tissues (Nakata et al., 2012), we suggest a general scenario in which KAN and HD-ZIPIII genes repress auxin response where they are expressed, leaving a narrow domain of auxin responsive cells in between their expression domains.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data and cited studies.

claim: A computational model incorporating the polarization of PIN1 towards cells with high intracellular auxin concentrations and assuming that both KAN1 and REV repress auxin-induced transcription can self-organize the periodic formation of auxin maxima along the boundary.
source: We tested this proposal in silico by implementing a previous model for phyllotaxis (Jönsson et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2006), now supported experimentally (Bayer et al., 2009; Bhatia et al., 2016; Heisler et al., 2010), that incorporates the polarization of PIN1 towards cells with high intracellular auxin concentrations. By assuming that both KAN1 and REV repress auxin-induced transcription and by including a narrow region of cells located between the KAN1 and REV expression domains the model was able to self-organize the periodic formation of auxin maxima along the boundary as predicted, compared to a broader distribution of maxima when such boundaries are not included (Figure 9A–D; compare 9B to 9D).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results presented in Figure 9.

claim: Auxin promotes the expression of several HD-ZIPIII genes in rice.
source: Indeed, auxin promotes the expression of several HD-ZIPIII genes in rice (Itoh et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In Arabidopsis, REV expression typically extends towards PIN1 polarity convergence patterns in the meristem periphery and disappears in axil regions where auxin is depleted.
source: and in Arabidopsis, REV expression typically extends towards PIN1 polarity convergence patterns in the meristem periphery and disappears in axil regions where auxin is depleted (Heisler et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The region in between the REV and KAN1 domains narrows due to a significant expansion of REV expression within 15 hr of combined NAA and NPA treatment.
source: We found that the region in between the REV and KAN1 domains narrowed due to a significant expansion of REV expression within 15 hr of treatment (Figure 10A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 10.

claim: REV becomes expressed in cells between the primordia and meristem where REV had presumably reduced its expression previously after auxin treatment.
source: REV also became expressed in cells between the primordia and meristem where REV had presumably reduced its expression previously (Figure 10C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 10.

claim: Although KAN expression appears static, more cells express REV after auxin treatment.
source: This was confirmed by following cells over time where we found that although KAN expression appeared static, more cells expressed REV (Figure 10C–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 10.

claim: A more subtle response of REV to auxin is observed as early as 6 hr upon combined NAA and NPA application.
source: A more subtle response was observed as early as 6 hr upon combined NAA and NPA application (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Local application of IAA to pin1-4 meristems results in a local response by REV within 16 hr of auxin application.
source: Local application of IAA to pin1-4 meristems also resulted in a local response by REV within 16 hr of auxin application (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exogenous auxin has little effect on a pCLV3:GFP-ER marker for central zone identity.
source: In contrast, exogenous auxin had little effect on a pCLV3:GFP-ER marker for central zone identity (Figure 10—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 10—figure supplement 3.

claim: Over the course of 48 hr after auxin treatment, KAN1 expression does not appear as expected in between the meristem and floral bracts of stages i1 and i2 at the time of treatment.
source: Apart from changes in REV we noticed that over the course of 48 hr, KAN1 expression did not appear as expected in between the meristem and floral bracts of stages i1 and i2 (but not P1) at the time of treatment (Figure 10I and J), compared to mock treated plants (Figure 10K and H), where KAN expression appeared adjacent to the primordia within 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 10.

claim: In vegetative meristems, contiguous REV expression often appears between the meristem and developing leaves where KAN1 expression would normally be expressed after auxin treatment.
source: In vegetative meristems this was more obvious where contiguous REV expression often appeared between the meristem and developing leaves where KAN1 expression would normally be expressed (Figure 11A–H; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 11 and Video 2.

claim: Exogenous auxin promotes HD-ZIPIII expression locally.
source: These results indicate exogenous auxin promotes HD-ZIPIII expression locally
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Exogenous auxin can prevent the establishment of KAN1 expression if applied at stages i1 and i2 of organ development.
source: and that exogenous auxin can prevent the establishment of KAN1 expression if applied at stages i1 and i2 of organ development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: After 18 hr of auxinole treatment, KAN expression expands slightly toward the meristem center.
source: To test whether REV or KAN1 expression depend on endogenous auxin for their patterns of expression we treated triple marker plants with the TIR1 antagonist auxinole (Hayashi et al., 2012) and found that after 18 hr of treatment KAN expression had expanded slightly toward the meristem center (Figure 12A and B; Figure 12—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 12.

claim: Combined treatment with auxinole, yucasin, and kyn leads to an arrest of organogenesis and 'pin' phenotype as well as a much more significant expansion and restriction of KAN1 and REV expression centrally, respectively.
source: This combination of treatments led to an arrest of organogenesis and 'pin' phenotype as well as a much more significant expansion and restriction of KAN1 and REV expression centrally, respectively (Figure 12C and D; Figure 12—figure supplement 1E–H Figure 12—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 12 and supplementary figures.

claim: KAN1 expression expands into cells originally located between the REV and KAN1 domains and cells that had previously been expressing REV at high levels after combined auxin depletion treatment.
source: KAN expression not only expanded into those cells originally located between the REV and KAN1 domains but also cells that had previously been expressing REV at high levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: KAN1 expression remains excluded from the central most cells of the shoot and established floral bracts and leaf primordia after auxin depletion.
source: However KAN1 expression remained excluded from the central most cells of the shoot and established floral bracts and leaf primordia, where REV expression still remained (Figure 12D; Figure 12—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 12 and supplementary figures.

claim: Combined inhibitor treatment confirms a strong decrease in overall intracellular auxin levels, including in the central meristem region and maturing organs.
source: Monitoring the ratiometric auxin sensor R2D2 in response to a similar combined inhibitor treatment confirmed a strong decrease in overall intracellular auxin levels, including in the central meristem region and maturing organs (Figure 12E and F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 12.

claim: Auxin independent mechanisms regulate the expression patterns of REV and KAN in the central zone and in organs after their initiation.
source: indicating that auxin independent mechanisms regulate the expression patterns of these genes in the central zone and in organs after their initiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Auxin depletion does not influence size of the central zone, as marked by the expression of pCLV3:GFP-ER.
source: In contrast to REV and KAN1, auxin depletion did not influence size of the central zone, as marked by the expression of pCLV3:GFP-ER (Figure 12—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 12—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dynamic changes in auxin levels specifically within the meristem periphery play a central role in regulating dorsal and ventral identities.
source: Overall these data indicate that dynamic changes in auxin levels specifically within the meristem periphery play a central role in regulating dorsal and ventral identities.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: High levels of auxin act to both trigger and maintain HD-ZIPIII expression, but only in cells not already expressing KAN1.
source: While high levels of auxin act to both trigger and maintain HD-ZIPIII expression, this only occurs in cells not already expressing KAN1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: High levels of auxin prevent the acropetal expansion of KAN1 expression, not only in cells within primordia but also in regions between the primordia and meristem.
source: Such high levels of auxin also prevent the acropetal expansion of KAN1 expression, not only in cells within primordia but also in regions between the primordia and meristem.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Once cells are exposed to low auxin levels, their fate becomes determined, i.e subsequent auxin exposure cannot reverse their trajectory towards ventral or peripheral cell identity.
source: As our auxin treatments only prevented KAN1 expression from establishing around primordia at stages, i1 and i2 and not around P1, which corresponds to a stage when auxin depletion has already occurred (Heisler et al., 2005), our data also suggest that once cells are exposed to low auxin levels, their fate becomes determined, i.e subsequent auxin exposure cannot reverse their trajectory towards ventral or peripheral cell identity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and cited studies.

claim: Outside the meristem periphery, both in the meristem central zone and within more established organs, REV and KAN expression appears comparatively auxin insensitive.
source: Outside the meristem periphery, both in the meristem central zone and within more established organs, REV and KAN expression appears comparatively auxin insensitive.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Wounding causes repolarization of PIN1 away from wound sites resulting in auxin depletion.
source: Since auxin is required to maintain REV at the expense of KAN expression in the meristem periphery and wounding causes repolarization of PIN1 away from wound sites (Heisler et al., 2010) resulting in auxin depletion (Landrein et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Auxin levels decrease in the vicinity of wounds.
source: Firstly, using a pulsed IR laser to ablate cells adjacent to young organ primordia we confirmed that auxin levels decrease in the vicinity of wounds by monitoring the expression of the R2D2 ratiometric marker (Figure 13A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 13.

claim: KAN1 becomes expressed in cells adjacent to the wound on either side, regardless of wound orientation with respect to the SAM.
source: We found that KAN1 became expressed in cells adjacent to the wound on either side, regardless of wound orientation with respect to the SAM (Figure 13C and D; Figure 13—figure supplement 1A–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 13 and supplementary figures.

claim: The induction of KAN1 expression around wounds can be completely eliminated if NAA and NPA are combined.
source: To test this hypothesis, we repeated these experiments while treating the wounded meristems with combinations of NAA and NPA over a 48 hr period and found that the induction of KAN1 expression around wounds could be completely eliminated if NAA and NPA were combined (Figure 13E–G; Figure 13—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 13 and supplementary figures.

claim: Wounds re-pattern peripheral cell identities due to the depletion of auxin in their vicinity.
source: Altogether then, our results strongly indicate that wounds re-pattern peripheral cell identities due to the depletion of auxin in their vicinity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Auxin depletion triggers a local commitment to peripheral cell fate (which includes expressing KAN1).
source: Specifically, we propose that auxin depletion triggers a local commitment to peripheral cell fate (which includes expressing KAN1), thereby providing a parsimonious explanation for the wound-associated disruptions to leaf polarity observed by Sussex and others (Sussex, 1955).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data and cited studies.

claim: Organs are pre-patterned by domains of KAN and HD-ZIPIII expression not only in terms of their differentiation but also their position and morphology.
source: Our results support elements of these latter proposals by revealing that organs are pre-patterned by domains of KAN and HD-ZIPIII expression not only in terms of their differentiation but also their position and morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The spatial arrangement of HD-ZIPIII and KAN expression present within organ founder cells is incorporated into organs as they initiate and directs patterns of morphogenesis.
source: The effect of ectopic KAN1 expression at the centre of the shoot on subsequent leaf positioning and growth is particularly striking and indicates that the spatial arrangement of HD-ZIPIII and KAN expression present within organ founder cells is incorporated into organs as they initiate and directs patterns of morphogenesis (Figure 7P–S; Figure 14).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 7 and Figure 14.

claim: The exact configuration of the HD-ZIPIII and KAN pre-pattern, including its propagation into developing organs, is dynamic and depends on changing auxin levels.
source: However, the exact configuration of this pre-pattern, including its propagation into developing organs, is dynamic and depends on changing auxin levels, although this regulation is unlikely to be direct.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: At sites of incipient organ formation, where auxin is concentrated in between the two expression domains, HD-ZIPIII expression is promoted and can expand peripherally, but only in cells adaxial to where KAN is expressed.
source: While high auxin levels promote HD-ZIPIII and represses KAN1 this is only true for cells not already expressing KAN1. Hence, at sites of incipient organ formation, where auxin is concentrated in between the two expression domains, HD-ZIPIII expression is promoted and can expand peripherally, but only in cells adaxial to where KAN is expressed.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: High levels of auxin prevent KAN expression from expanding acropetally into HD-ZIPIII expressing cells, causing the boundary to remain relatively static with respect to the underlying cells.
source: At the same time, this high level of auxin prevents KAN expression from expanding acropetally into HD-ZIPIII expressing cells, causing the boundary to remain relatively static with respect to the underlying cells (Figure 14A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and presented in Figure 14.

claim: If auxin levels drop, HD-ZIPIII expression decreases and KAN expression takes its place.
source: However if auxin levels drop, for instance when PIN1 reverses polarity away from cells between the meristem and primordium (Heisler et al., 2005; Qi et al., 2014), HD-ZIPIII expression decreases and KAN expression takes its place (Figure 14B and C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data, cited studies, and presented in Figure 14.

claim: High levels of auxin 'lock-in' the spatial arrangement of HD-ZIPIII and KAN expression within organ founder cells at organ inception until a later stage when the pattern becomes auxin independent.
source: Hence high levels of auxin 'lock-in' the spatial arrangement of HD-ZIPIII and KAN expression within organ founder cells at organ inception until a later stage when the pattern becomes auxin independent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: In between primordia, where auxin levels are lower, cells continuously transition from expressing REV in the central zone to expressing KAN1 as they are displaced peripherally.
source: In between primordia, where auxin levels are lower, cells continuously transition from expressing REV in the central zone (where HD-ZIPIII expression appears auxin insensitive) to expressing KAN1 as they are displaced peripherally, as also indicated by the expression patterns of these genes in pin1 meristems (Figure 10—figure supplement 2A,E and I).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: The dorsoventral patterning of organs results from a four-step process: (i) signals during embryonic development establish concentric patterns of Class III HD-ZIP and KAN gene expression; (ii) the boundary between these domains helps to define sites for auxin-dependent organogenesis i.e. the meristem peripheral zone; (iii) As organs form, dynamic auxin levels modulate the patterns of HD-ZIPIII and KAN expression, thereby helping to position new organs and establish their dorsoventrality; (iv) patterns of HD-ZIPIII and KAN gene expression within organs are stabilized and dictate future patterns of morphogenesis.
source: Overall these results imply that the dorsoventral patterning of organs results from a four-step process: (i) signals during embryonic development establish concentric patterns of Class III HD-ZIP and KAN gene expression; (ii) the boundary between these domains helps to define sites for auxin-dependent organogenesis i.e. the meristem peripheral zone; (iii) As organs form, dynamic auxin levels modulate the patterns of HD-ZIPIII and KAN expression, thereby helping to position new organs and establish their dorsoventrality; (iv) patterns of HD-ZIPIII and KAN gene expression within organs are stabilized and dictate future patterns of morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a proposed model summarizing the findings from the experimental data.

claim: Wounds in the meristem outer cell layer specifically alter cell polarities such that PIN1 becomes polarized away from wounds in adjacent cells, leading to auxin depletion.
source: Wounds in the meristem outer cell layer specifically alter cell polarities such that PIN1 becomes polarized away from wounds in adjacent cells (Heisler et al., 2010), leading to auxin depletion (Landrein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KAN1 is upregulated and REV is repressed around wounds.
source: Consistent with this, we observe KAN1 to be upregulated and REV to be repressed around wounds.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: Changes in KAN1 and REV expression around wounds can be completely blocked by auxin application.
source: Furthermore, such changes can be completely blocked by auxin application.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: Transient high levels of auxin inhibit establishment or maintenance of dorsal fate and/or promote establishment or maintenance of ventral cell fate in tomato.
source: Our conclusion that auxin promotes dorsal cell fate while inhibiting ventral cell fate contrasts with those of another study reporting that transient high levels of auxin inhibit establishment or maintenance of dorsal fate and/or promote establishment or maintenance of ventral cell fate (Qi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In pin and pid mutants, lower auxin levels may result in lower expression levels of REV and possibly other Class III HD-ZIPs, leading to leaf ventralization.
source: Although our results cannot easily explain the tomato data, since we find that high auxin levels are required to maintain REV expression during organ establishment, we would expect that in pin and pid mutants, lower auxin levels may well result in lower expression levels of REV and possibly other Class III HD-ZIPs, leading to leaf ventralization as reported in these mutant backgrounds (Qi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental data and cited studies.

claim: Organ initiation requires high auxin levels but auxin can only trigger organogenesis in the peripheral zone where the HD-ZIPIII/KAN boundary occurs.
source: For instance, organ initiation requires high auxin levels but auxin can only trigger organogenesis in the peripheral zone (Reinhardt et al., 2000) where the HD-ZIPIII/KAN boundary occurs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and the experimental data.

claim: Auxin application results in growth but only from the leaf margins, corresponding to a DV boundary.
source: A similar relationship holds for leaves where auxin application results in growth but only from the leaf margins, again corresponding to a DV boundary (Koenig et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DR5 expression appears higher at DV boundaries compared to the broader predicted auxin distribution, as marked by R2D2.
source: We further show that the localization of auxin response to DV boundaries applies generally, i.e. DR5 expression appears higher at such boundaries compared to the broader predicted auxin distribution, as marked by R2D2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: The locations of PIN1 polarity convergences correspond to a region of cells in between the expression domains of HD-ZIPIII and KAN where their expression is low or absent.
source: Imaging data reveals that the locations of PIN1 polarity convergences correspond to a region of cells in between the expression domains of HD-ZIPIII and KAN where their expression is low or absent.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data described in the text.

claim: Both the HD-ZIPIII and KAN genes repress auxin activity.
source: Given our results as well as genetic and molecular data indicating that both the HD-ZIPIII and KAN genes repress auxin activity (Huang et al., 2014; Merelo et al., 2013; Müller et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Localized absence of HD-ZIPIII and KAN expression results in a local de-repression of auxin-induced transcription.
source: we propose that this localized absence of expression results in a local de-repression of auxin-induced transcription.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data and cited studies.

claim: Localized auxin activity orients cell polarity, including microtubule orientations, in a non-cell autonomous manner.
source: Such localized auxin activity has recently been shown to orient cell polarity, including microtubule orientations, in a non-cell autonomous manner (Bhatia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The ability of dorsoventral boundaries to act as organizers rests in-part on their ability to orient cell polarity non-cell autonomously by localizing auxin activity.
source: Hence, we suggest that the proposed ability of dorsoventral boundaries to act as organizers analogous to those of the Drosophila wing (Diaz-Benjumea and Cohen, 1993; Waites and Hudson, 1995) rests in-part on their ability to orient cell polarity non-cell autonomously by localizing auxin activity (Figure 14D).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data, cited studies, and presented in Figure 14.

claim: The resulting growth from localized auxin activity may occur either in a periodic fashion along the boundary typical of phyllotaxis and complex leaves, or in a more continuous manner typical of simple leaves, depending on the strength of auxin transport or other modifications to the cell polarity feedback system.
source: The resulting growth may occur either in a periodic fashion along the boundary typical of phyllotaxis and complex leaves, or in a more continuous manner typical of simple leaves, depending on the strength of auxin transport or other modifications to the cell polarity feedback system (Bilsborough et al., 2011; Koenig et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental data and cited studies.
